summary: The Home Appliance Protection and Affordability Act changes how the Department of Energy (DOE) creates and updates energy and water efficiency standards for household appliances and other consumer products. The bill adds strict new requirements the DOE must follow before issuing rules, such as proving that a standard will not increase net costs for consumers, will pay for itself within three years through utility savings, and will not reduce product performance or eliminate certain fuel-type products from the market. It also sets rules for revoking standards through a petition process, prohibits new standards for distribution transformers, requires public disclosure of certain DOE meetings, and allows specific new standards for clothes washers and dishwashers.

affected_groups.effect: Will experience appliance standards built around stricter economic justifications, ensuring that product purchase, installation, and maintenance cost increases are outweighed by energy or water savings within three years.
Will face new economic, technological, performance, and petition-based criteria that govern how federal energy efficiency rules are written, evaluated, and potentially revoked.

Must alter its rulemaking timelines, perform detailed economic impact studies, exclude greenhouse gas calculations, and publicly disclose specific past meetings before issuing appliance efficiency standards.

key_provisions: Requires the DOE to conduct a quantitative economic impact analysis before setting any new or amended energy conservation standard, including evaluations of low-income household costs and regional variations.

Prohibits the DOE from declaring a standard economically justified unless it results in no net costs to consumers and generates energy or water savings within three years that exceed any increased product costs.
Bans the DOE from considering estimates of social costs or social benefits associated with incremental greenhouse gas emissions when determining if a standard is economically justified.

Establishes a petition process allowing the Secretary of Energy to revoke or amend standards that cost consumers extra, do not meaningfully conserve resources, are not technologically feasible, or cause certain products to disappear from the market.
Prohibits the Secretary of Energy from issuing any new or revised energy conservation standards for distribution transformers.

Mandates that the DOE publicly disclose meetings held over the preceding five years with any entity that has ties to China or the Chinese Communist Party, has produced studies or advocated for energy restrictions, and has received federal funds.
Explicitly permits the DOE to prescribe certain new or amended energy and water conservation standards for clothes washers and dishwashers.
summary_detail.plain_summary: The Home Appliance Protection and Affordability Act changes how the Department of Energy (DOE) creates and updates energy and water efficiency standards for household appliances and other consumer products. The bill adds strict new requirements the DOE must follow before issuing rules, such as proving that a standard will not increase net costs for consumers, will pay for itself within three years through utility savings, and will not reduce product performance or eliminate certain fuel-type products from the market. It also sets rules for revoking standards through a petition process, prohibits new standards for distribution transformers, requires public disclosure of certain DOE meetings, and allows specific new standards for clothes washers and dishwashers.
summary_detail.significance: This bill significantly alters federal regulatory authority over consumer products by restricting how the Department of Energy weighs economic and environmental factors when writing appliance efficiency standards. It establishes mandatory cost-benefit floors for consumers, limits future rules on distribution transformers, and creates explicit avenues to roll back existing appliance regulations.
